Justin Brierley contributes substantive arguments, including victim-centered challenges, incarnation as solidarity and the N. T. Wright why/response framing. Explicit editorial approval keeps the primary speakers’ replies eligible but assigns no host claim, host-read passage or outside quotation to a primary speaker. Their actual adoption and reasons, not the host’s framing, determine any selected claim. Audit unequal prompting fairly.

Host-read quotation from Ehrman’s book at about 56:52–58:22 is context, not a speech or quotation delivered by Ehrman. His subsequent own explanation is eligible. Do not transfer the host’s quoted wording into a participant quote.

Swinburne defines omnipotence as logical possibility, distinguishing the surgeon’s physical constraints from divine logical constraints. His positive value is free and responsible choice with consequences, not choice without effects.

Swinburne conditions creator authority on victims having an overall beneficial life or other benefits. Later he calls involuntary usefulness a good for its subject but explicitly not necessarily an overwhelming or greatest good, and says it is not his only reason. Preserve these qualifications instead of attributing a blanket justification of every atrocity.

Ehrman recognizes the free-will account is only the first stage of Swinburne’s explanation and grants much suffering comes from human treatment of others. He challenges the explanatory reach to natural evil, starving victims and heaven. Preserve those concessions.

The Holocaust exchange contains overlapping turns. Ehrman says victims did not choose to suffer, rejects the benefit justification, and distinguishes human perpetrators from divine involvement. Swinburne distinguishes opportunities for goodness from actual goodness, and permission from directly killing, while appealing to historically consequential choices. Do not replace either position with the other speaker’s characterization.

Swinburne appeals to biblical diversity for different evils, Hebrews 12, John 9 and permission of hostile forces. Ehrman argues some authorial views conflict. Swinburne prioritizes church interpretation; Ehrman prioritizes the authors’ historical expectations. These positions must not be silently reconciled from outside research.

Swinburne separates incarnation as shared suffering from redemption as reparation and stresses Christ’s life and consequent death. His claim does not guarantee an immediate end to suffering. Ehrman presses apparent nonintervention and imminent-kingdom expectations; Swinburne answers with resurrection, an acknowledged early expectation and parables allowing delay.

Ehrman’s closing says we CAN respond to suffering despite lacking a perfectly satisfying explanation. The caption we can’t have a response is a recognition error resolved by the supplementary audio check. Do not quote the corrupted caption or infer passivity, helplessness or a contradiction from it.

Swinburne answers the heaven objection in his last summary, distinguishing sequential goods of self-formation and a subsequently good character, then offers the prebirth choice illustration. Ehrman has no later reply opportunity. A reply deficit cannot be inferred from this speaking order.
